The chord-to-radius ratio (c/R) ranged from 0.25 to 0.74 in the experiments.
Increasing c/R led to higher virtual camber and virtual incidence.
More negative preset pitch angles (α_p) were found to be optimal as c/R increased.
Positive geometric camber enhanced upstream performance, while negative camber reduced downstream losses.
The experiments were conducted at diameter-based Reynolds numbers between approximately 1.6 × 10^5 and 2.7 × 10^5.
The optimal performance at a given net camber was found to occur at a relatively constant net incidence of 0° to +1°.
The paper proposes using net camber (γ_net) and net incidence (α_net) as composite variables to better understand turbine performance and design behavior.
The study used two experimental datasets: one varying preset pitch, c/R, blade count, and Reynolds number, and the other examining geometric blade camber and pitch.
The blockage ratio was approximately 11% across all tests.
The blade height (h) and outermost diameter (D_o) were held constant at 23.4 cm and ~17.2 cm, respectively.
The optimal tip-speed ratio ranged from 2.3 to 3.6, with the highest values for low c/R and the lowest for high c/R.
Increasing toe-out preset pitch (more negative α_p) reduced upstream performance but increased downstream performance.
Increasing net camber, whether through virtual or geometric means, had similar effects on phase-averaged performance.
Changes in c/R, preset pitch, and camber all exhibited comparable magnitudes of influence on turbine performance.
Reynolds number effects were considered secondary compared to the primary geometric parameters.
